If You Want to Kill Yourself
Maybe you’re reading this about to act, or with the means close by. Then before anything else, get another human being involved, and put some distance between you and the means. A crisis line counts, and the person on the other end can be a total stranger. Do the same if you can’t stop yourself, and also when you’re badly disoriented or intoxicated, or can’t tell whether any of this is you. Getting safe first keeps the question of whether life is worth living open long enough to look at.
Then, before getting all philosophical, make sure there’s a real, live grown-up in the room or on the phone, if that’s possible. And as for the internal psychology of it, when the part that wants to die feels like all of you, go ahead and notice who’s doing the noticing (as we discussed in Noticing Counts), or borrow an adult from the adult lending library in your head :). Any part of you that can help keep your body safe, or would rather wait on a decision you can’t undo, is welcome. And if none of them shows up yet? No problem, the questions can wait.

rewrite:
How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?
What do you picture when you wish someone well? Probably them fed and safe, with people around who like them, stuff like that. Wanting that for somebody is love (babies get this part already), and practical love matters a lot. The horizon of what I can wish for someone is partly shaped by the happiness, peace, and freedom I know are possible.
But maybe you’ve had a big spiritual experience, and for a while you felt a peace or a love you didn’t know existed. After that, “I want you to be happy” can mean something much bigger, almost overnight. That’s why loving-kindness meditation can sound comically simple to someone who’s never been near that, and so powerful to someone who has. Saying “may you be happy” over and over won’t zap you into profound love, but it’s one way people find that love and grow it.
If that bigger happiness makes you curious, I’d follow the curiosity and skip pretending to believe anything. Read people from a few different traditions, say a Sufi poet and a Zen teacher. And if you ever meet someone who’s happy in a way that doesn’t add up, watch how they treat people on a day when everything’s going wrong for them.
Sometimes your little one has enough care, and what’s missing is something else. A hot meal can help, and so can saying no to your boss, but is that actually targeting the deeper existential question underneath? Life shouldn’t be just something you endure, like a hamster wheel or a rat race. What would you need to bring zest to a life of discovery?
Curiosity can be enough here, something like “Other people say they’ve felt a depth of love or peace that I never have. I don’t know if I believe their explanation. But what if the experience is possible for me?”

Some families run on a bargain like “If I’m happy while someone I love is suffering, I’m abandoning them.”
That’s exactly why I was crying for 14 years. Beginning at the age of 12, when I really started to understand that life is brutal for most people, I became convinced that being happy myself, while others weren’t, was selfish. I had this poster in my room that really resonated with me, by the famous socialist, Eugene V. Debs. I told this to a therapist in college and she actually agreed it was a good reason to be depressed!
What I found, once I started cultivating my own happiness, was that I got a lot better at helping other people toward theirs. That might not be how it goes for everyone, and it doesn’t mean unhappy people can’t help. Do your part for people who are suffering, and skip the part where you have to be miserable too.
Some friends or family really might not like it when you get happier, though. Someone might pull away, or keep dragging you back into the old misery. I’d take that loss seriously, and look at what they do and what you owe them, before deciding it’s envy.
I’d still try a small good thing, like a nice meal, and see what actually happens.

rewrite:
Pattern 10: Meta Model questions — the de-hypnosis tool
To 'Milton Model' is to open things up, so the listener can fill in what fits for them. To 'Meta Model' is to stop and ask, "What do you mean by that?" In order to be ethical with people, you need to do both.
When something sounds true but vague, ask, "What do you mean, specifically?" Then find out according to who, and compared to what. If you hear "always" or "never," check whether it's really every time. If someone's afraid of doing something, ask what exactly would happen if they did. And ask how they know, and what evidence would change their mind.
So when someone is starting to tense up in their body, use the Milton Model to help them soften. And when you feel you're losing track of what's really going on, that's the time for the Meta Model.

I think the opposite trap can feel a lot like finally having your act together. It’s forced adulthood, and it sounds like “Nope, all good!” from somebody with a fever who’s cleaning the whole kitchen anyway. Not a lot of fun in that kitchen, and nobody gets very close to the person in it. If that’s you, clamping down harder is going to feel like the fix, but it’s just more of the same. I’d try croaking to someone you trust, “Could you pick up some soup?” If you keep swinging between spoiling and clamping down, try staying warm while you say what happens next, like “Not now, we’ll go after lunch.”
Once a need does show, after all that hiding, it’s okay to want a lot of closeness. So then someone you love goes for a walk alone, and you’ve texted “hello??” before they’re at the corner. When they get back, you sulk all night. Wanting them close is fine! Blowing up their phone and sulking all night is a different story. Your Guide could help you ask for what you need instead, like a hug before they go and a rough idea of when they’ll be back. Before any of that, though, I’d let your little one say what’s going on. I think it just wants to know they’re coming back.
The Guide doesn’t need to know everything for sure (that would be an OCD Guide, and then you’d need a Guide for the OCD Guide). It chooses the next sane step that fits your values based on the info available, and that’s how it helps your little one grow toward a whole life. Waiting to be sure first is sometimes proper & prudent, but if it’s a pattern, it can keep life on hold, and then your little one’s world stays small. Sometimes something really is stuck on someone else’s end (you’ve asked, and followed up, and there’s nothing left for you to do yet), and waiting on that isn’t avoidance. The Guide can let it wait, keeping an eye out for when it frees up, and keep the rest of your life moving, so your little one keeps growing anyway.

rewrite:
Differentiation can happen right inside a family, religion, community or relationship. You’d still belong, just selectively. As a differentiated adult you can stay deeply embedded, free to question things or disagree. If a parent used to go quiet and hurt whenever you disagreed, that might be hard to believe. A family where everyone gets to be their own person is healthier than an enmeshed one, and a faith that’s your own is healthier than religious compliance. It can be the same religion either way. And two differentiated people have a sturdier relationship than two who’ve been absorbed into each other.
Day to day, differentiation looks something like this:
- Caring about somebody’s feelings without automatically adopting their opinions or sacrificing your own ground. Their reasons can still change your mind, though.
- Noticing when you agreed in the moment and disagree later: “Wait, why was I nodding along?”
- Noticing when what you thought you knew suddenly feels like water dripping through your hand because of praise or pity, fear or attraction, or something that really resonates with you.
- Disappointing people and withstanding social pressure, and still being recognizably yourself wherever you are (maybe louder in some places). That one can take a while.
- Questioning what you were programmed to believe while holding the discomfort, and without having to stop loving anyone over it.
Differentiation is slow, and it goes on your whole life. Sometimes you need to take a break from a family, group or relationship, even if they aren’t doing anything to you. Simply being around them may pull you into that programmed space where listening to what you really want becomes harder. Some people come back later on different terms, and sometimes the break has to be long-term because the pattern of losing yourself with them is deeply entrenched. As you differentiate, you learn to tell which of those apply.
Key developed this identity and differentiation portion of the method, drawing on Murray Bowen’s family-systems work and her own self-therapy.

Remember When You Already Did It
My father often suggested folks remember a similar-level (or even harder) challenge that they were able to handle. Maybe you survived a car crash and surgery a few years ago, but now you’re having trouble with emotional eating. You can draw strength from the past. As my sister, a historian, likes to say, “The past didn’t go anywhere.” Your own challenge can be less dramatic than a car crash, as long as it really happened. So who or what helped you get through it? Is one piece of that still within reach? If you catch yourself thinking “I survived a car crash, so why can’t I stop eating when I’m upset?”, that’s the past turned into a stick to hit yourself with. Maybe you’re more worn out now, or missing whatever helped back then. (If no example comes to mind, try another doorway.)

rewrite:
The 15-minute daily practice
You don't need to learn a second script for this. It's the same process (gather your attention, notice what's here, respond, wait, and come all the way back), just for fifteen minutes or so. That is long enough to induce yourself (it only takes a few minutes), practice and let it unfold at its own pace, and come out again (that takes a few minutes too). Fifteen minutes is just a handy appointment with yourself, though, and your feelings don't have to keep to it. Five minutes is plenty to see what happens when you simply sit in silence, listening, and you can interrupt yourself at any time to change direction if that feels better.
You can also try other ways of inducing yourself, such as becoming aware of 3 things you can see, 3 things you can hear, 3 things you can feel in your body; then 2 of each, 1 of each. Then count from 5 to 1 and begin to listen. Choose one way to induce yourself. You don't need to try all of them (in fact, stacking them might be counterproductive).
Once you have practiced listening a few times with the recordings, you may want to shorten them to speed up your induction, or even practice without playing them back at all. On the other hand, if you like using the recordings, there is no reason to stop. (Once you know the induction well, the cue from "A shortcut back into hypnosis" can shorten it too.)
As you come out of the process, ask yourself what needed warmth, what needed to be protected, what you need to do differently to be more in accord with truth and love and life. Is there something you want to explore more fully or a capacity you want to build? And most importantly, what can you now carry yourself that you used to have to borrow? If you identified something you needed to do differently, make a plan with yourself to do that thing. The more specific you can be, the more likely you are to change: “If _________ (fill in the cue for the old pattern), then I will do ________ (fill in a small action that will begin to change the pattern).” Then check back later and see how you are doing – sleeping, relating, functioning, etc., not only how impressive the session felt.

First Social Connections, Done Right
Then there are people you’re just getting to know. Meeting them can turn into a kind of test--”First impressions are everything,” as they say, but it could be even worse than that, if you need them to prove you’re lovable. Nobody’s a reassurance machine. I’m giving you permission now to quit school and flunk the tests. Get curious about who this person is, and who you are, and let both of you have your own reasons for being there in the beautiful present. Leaning on each other is still a big part of relationships, and it goes both ways.
I can’t tell you where to look for people who fit you, but I’d bet on more than one place. Keep the good people you’ve already got. Then maybe try a class, or a spiritual community if one really fits you. Not every one of them has to click (nobody’s taking attendance). And if any group, or any one person, starts acting like they should be your only support, that’s where I’d want the Protector paying attention.
The same goes for doctors. If a hospital held you against your will, or a treatment hurt you, no wonder asking for help feels scary. Bring someone you trust to speak up for you (it doesn’t have to be the relative who never respected your wishes), and ask what a treatment’s for.

rewrite:
Journal With Each Hand
Lucia Capacchione, an art therapist, wrote a whole book on this one, The Power of Your Other Hand. As titles go, it’s pretty literal. Your other hand, the clumsy one, writes like a first grader anyway, so it gets the scared or hurt feelings. The usual hand answers, as the grown-up. Some people who get nothing but silence from their little one are surprised by what the other hand comes up with. A protective part might grab the pen first, and then it gets that hand until it’s had its say.
And what if all that writing leaves you more confused than when you started? Then just keep track for a while, and save the patterns for later, if they turn out to matter at all. A memory aid doesn’t have to explain your life. It could be a dated note of what happened, or of what helped. A reminder or a next step works too. Or you can leave yourself a voice note.
